title: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
summary: From XOR and the one-time pad to AES modes, AEAD, hashes, HMAC, password hashing, randomness, Diffie-Hellman, RSA and signatures, taught through the real failures they caused.
outcomes: Explain confidentiality, integrity and authenticity and pick the primitive that gives each
Explain why ECB leaks patterns and why nonce or key reuse breaks CTR, GCM and ECDSA
Compute toy Diffie-Hellman and RSA by hand and say why real use needs authentication and padding
Use AEAD, HMAC, slow password hashes and a CSPRNG correctly in Python
Trace real failures (Adobe, Debian OpenSSL, Flame, SHAttered, PS3, CurveBall) to the rule each broke
Review crypto code for nonce reuse, weak randomness, broken hashes, unchecked parameters and == on secrets

lessons.title: What cryptography promises, and to whom

blocks.md:
Picture Alice sending Bob a message that says "pay 100 to Carol" across a network neither of them controls. Three different things can go wrong. Someone can **read** it. Someone can **change** it to "pay 900 to Carol". Or someone can send a message that only **claims** to come from Alice.

Cryptography is the set of mathematical tools that guard against these three. In this course we call the passive listener **Eve** (an eavesdropper: someone who only listens) and the active attacker who changes, drops or forges messages **Mallory**. Alice and Bob as names for the two honest parties go back at least to the 1978 RSA paper by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, which wrote "A and B (also known as Alice and Bob)".

The three goals, with their usual names:

- **Confidentiality**: only the intended reader can understand the message. Defeats Eve.
- **Integrity**: any change to the message is detected. Defeats Mallory's edits.
- **Authenticity**: the receiver can tell who really sent it. Defeats Mallory's forgeries.

Two more words you will meet constantly: **plaintext** is the readable message, and **ciphertext** is the scrambled form that travels. A **key** is a secret value that, fed together with the plaintext into an **algorithm** (a fixed recipe), produces the ciphertext.

blocks.title: Who can do what on the wire

scenes.caption: Alice sends a plain message. Anyone with access to the network path sees it and can act on it.
Eve copies traffic without changing it. Only confidentiality (encryption) helps against Eve.
Mallory rewrites "100" to "900". Encryption alone does not stop this; integrity checks do (lessons 7 and 10).
Mallory sends a brand-new message signed "Alice". Authenticity (MACs and signatures) lets Bob reject it.

blocks.md:
**Kerckhoffs's principle.** In 1883 the cryptographer Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote a pair of articles in the French Journal des sciences militaires, "La cryptographie militaire" (military cryptography), listing rules for a usable cipher. The one that survived is the second: the system "must not require secrecy and can be stolen by the enemy without causing trouble". In modern words: assume the attacker knows your algorithm and your code. All the security must sit in the **key**.

This is why every primitive in this course (AES, SHA-256, HMAC, RSA) is public and standardised. Public algorithms get attacked by thousands of researchers, and the survivors earn trust. A secret home-made algorithm has only had its author look at it.

Misconception: "nobody knows our format, so it is safe". That is security through obscurity. Formats leak, binaries get reverse-engineered, employees leave. If learning the algorithm breaks your system, it was never secure.

What cryptography does **not** do: it does not stop someone who has your key, it does not fix a bug in the code that calls it, and it does not decide who should be trusted. Most real breaches in this course are **misuse**: the maths was fine, but a key was reused, a random number was not random, or a check was skipped. The rest of the course teaches each primitive and then exactly how it fails.
Ask of every design: which of confidentiality, integrity and authenticity do I need, against whom, and where does the key live? A primitive that gives one goal never silently gives the others.

blocks.question: A web form sends a price to the server over an encrypted connection, and the server trusts that price. A user edits the price in their own browser before sending. Which goal failed?
options: None of the cryptographic goals: the sender is the attacker, so the server must not trust client-supplied data
Confidentiality: the encryption was too weak
Integrity: the ciphertext was altered in transit
Authenticity: the server did not know who sent it
blocks.explain: The connection did its job: nobody in the middle read or changed anything. The attacker is the legitimate endpoint. Cryptography protects data between parties; it cannot make an untrusted party honest. That is an access control and validation problem.

blocks.question: By Kerckhoffs's principle, which of these should be treated as secret?
options: The source code of the encryption routine
blocks.explain: Only the key. Everything else should be assumed known to the attacker, because in practice it eventually is.

lessons.title: Bits, bytes, hex and XOR: the alphabet of cryptography

blocks.md:
Computers store everything as **bits** (binary digits): each is 0 or 1. Eight bits make a **byte**, which can hold 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 256 different values, 0 to 255. Text becomes bytes through a table: in ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) the letter H is 72, which is `01001000` in binary.

Long binary strings are hard to read, so engineers write bytes in **hexadecimal** (base sixteen): digits 0 to 9 then a to f. One hex digit covers exactly four bits, so one byte is always two hex digits. H is `0x48` (the `0x` prefix just means "hex follows"). Every key, hash and ciphertext in this course is shown in hex.

**XOR** (exclusive or) is one of the most used operations in symmetric cryptography (symmetric: the same secret key both encrypts and decrypts, unlike the public-key methods of lessons 13 to 15). It compares two bits and outputs 1 when exactly one of them is 1: "exclusive" because the case where both are 1 is excluded.

- 0 XOR 0 = 0
- 0 XOR 1 = 1
- 1 XOR 0 = 1
- 1 XOR 1 = 0

On bytes, XOR works bit by bit. Read it as: **wherever the key has a 1, flip the data bit**. Python writes it `^`; maths writes it $\oplus$.

blocks.title: XOR flips bits where the key has a 1

scenes.caption: One byte of data and one byte of key. We combine them position by position.
Where the key bit is 1 (positions 1, 2, 4, 5) the data bit flips. Where it is 0 the data bit passes through unchanged.
XOR the result with the same key and the same bits flip back: the original byte returns. This is why XOR can both encrypt and decrypt.
Without the key, the output 11011110 could have come from any data byte: for every possible data byte there is exactly one key that produces it.

blocks.tex: (m \oplus k) \oplus k = m \qquad m \oplus m = 0 \qquad m \oplus 0 = m
blocks.caption: The three facts behind every XOR trick in this course. The second one is also the root of the two-time pad disaster in lesson 4.

blocks.code:
a = 0b10110010              # one byte of data
k = 0b01101100              # one byte of key
c = a ^ k                   # ^ is XOR in Python
print(f"{c:08b}")           # 11011110
print(f"{c ^ k:08b}")       # 10110010: XOR with k again undoes it
print(f"{ord('H'):08b}", hex(ord('H')))   # 01001000 0x48
print(bytes([0x48, 0x69]))  # b'Hi'
blocks.caption: Runnable. XOR in Python is the ^ operator; f"{x:08b}" prints a byte as 8 bits.

blocks.md: **Modular arithmetic** appears later for public-key crypto, so meet it now. "$a \bmod n$" means the remainder when $a$ is divided by $n$. A 12-hour clock does arithmetic mod 12: 9 o'clock plus 5 hours is 2 o'clock, because $14 \bmod 12 = 2$. Results always stay in the range 0 to $n-1$, so numbers "wrap around" instead of growing. A byte is arithmetic mod 256 for the same reason: 255 + 1 wraps to 0.

blocks.prompt: If you XOR a byte with itself, what do you get, and why might that matter when the same key is used twice?
blocks.reveal: You get 0 (every bit meets an identical bit). So if two ciphertexts were made with the same key, XORing them together makes the key cancel: $(m_1 \oplus k) \oplus (m_2 \oplus k) = m_1 \oplus m_2$. Lesson 4 shows this leak with real bytes.

blocks.question: What is 0x0F XOR 0xFF?
blocks.explain: 0x0F is 00001111 and 0xFF is 11111111. Every bit of 0x0F is flipped by the all-ones key, giving 11110000, which is 0xF0.

blocks.question: What is 17 mod 5?
blocks.explain: 17 = 3 x 5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

lessons.title: Encoding, hashing and encryption are three different things

blocks.md: Engineers often say "we encrypted it" about data that was only encoded, or "we hashed the card numbers so they are encrypted". These are three different operations with different promises. The quickest way to tell them apart is to ask two questions: **does it use a key?** and **can it be reversed?**

- **Encoding** changes the representation so data survives a channel. Base64, for example, rewrites bytes using 64 safe printable characters so binary data can travel in email or JSON. No key, fully reversible by anyone. It gives **no** security.
- **Hashing** feeds data through a hash function that outputs a short fixed-size fingerprint (a **digest**). No key, and designed to be one-way: you cannot run it backwards. It gives integrity checks, not secrecy.
- **Encryption** uses a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext. Reversible, but only by someone with the right key. It gives confidentiality.

blocks.title: Same input, three operations

scenes.caption: Encoding: Base64 output looks scrambled but anyone can decode it with no secret. Never treat it as protection.
Hashing: SHA-256 gives a 256-bit fingerprint (first 8 bytes shown, computed). No key, and no way back except guessing inputs.
Encryption: the output depends on a key (and a random value), so it differs each time. Only the key holder can reverse it.

blocks.code:
import base64, hashlib
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

secret = b"hunter2"

# Encoding: no key, anyone can reverse it
enc = base64.b64encode(secret)
print(enc, base64.b64decode(enc))       # b'aHVudGVyMg==' b'hunter2'

# Hashing: no key, one way, same input gives same output
print(hashlib.sha256(secret).hexdigest()[:16])   # f52fbd32b2b3b86f

# Encryption: reversible, but only with the key
key = Fernet.generate_key()
token = Fernet(key).encrypt(secret)
print(Fernet(key).decrypt(token))       # b'hunter2'
blocks.caption: Runnable. Fernet is the cryptography library's ready-made recipe for authenticated symmetric encryption: AES in CBC mode plus an HMAC tag, which you meet in lessons 5, 6 and 10.

blocks.md: A hash of a short or guessable value is not secret. There are only 10,000 four-digit PINs; hashing all of them takes a fraction of a second, so a stored SHA-256 of a PIN is as good as the PIN. Lesson 11 covers how passwords must be stored instead.

A quick defender test when reviewing a system: find where sensitive data is stored and ask "what would an attacker who steals this table need to read it?" If the answer is "nothing" (encoding) or "a guessing loop" (fast hash of guessable data), the data is effectively exposed. If the answer is "the key, which lives in a separate key management service", you have real encryption.

blocks.question: A colleague stores API tokens Base64-encoded in the database "so they are not in plain text". What does an attacker who dumps the table need to use the tokens?
options: The encryption key from the application server
A large brute-force search of the token space
Nothing beyond a Base64 decoder, which every language ships
blocks.explain: Base64 is an encoding with no key. Decoding is instant and public. The tokens are effectively stored in plain text.

blocks.question: Which operation fits "I need to check later that this downloaded file has not changed, and secrecy does not matter"?
blocks.explain: A hash gives a short fingerprint that changes if the file changes. (Lesson 9 adds the caveat: an attacker who can also replace the published hash needs a signature to stop them.)

lessons.title: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key

blocks.md:
Take the XOR idea to its limit. Generate a key of truly random bytes **as long as the message**, XOR it with the message, and never use that key again. This is the **one-time pad**. Its first word says the rule: use once.

Tiny example: the message "Hi" is bytes `48 69`. With the random key `3c a7`, the ciphertext is `74 ce`. To Eve, `74 ce` is consistent with every possible two-byte message, because for any message there is exactly one key that would produce this ciphertext, and every key was equally likely.

In 1949 the mathematician Claude Shannon, in a paper in the Bell System Technical Journal, proved what this buys. A system has **perfect secrecy** if seeing the ciphertext tells the enemy nothing new about the message. Shannon showed perfect secrecy is possible, but needs at least as many possible keys as possible messages. The one-time pad meets that bound exactly, and the paper names it the Vernam system after the telegraph cipher G. S. Vernam described in a 1926 paper. No amount of computing power breaks it.

So why is it not used everywhere? Because the key must be as long as all the data you will ever send, delivered in advance over a secure channel, and never reused. That is impractical for the internet. Every practical cipher in the rest of this course trades perfect secrecy for a short key.

blocks.title: Two messages, one key: the key cancels out

scenes.caption: Two 5-byte messages in hex (ASCII). The sender lazily uses the same key bytes for both.
c1 = m1 XOR key. Alone, c1 is perfectly secret: it looks like random bytes.
c2 = m2 XOR key. Also random-looking on its own.
Eve XORs the two ciphertexts. The key cancels (k XOR k = 0) and Eve holds m1 XOR m2 = 1f 10 0b 75 18, with no key involved at all.
If Eve can guess any part of m1 (a header, a greeting), XORing it in reveals the matching part of m2. Real languages are predictable enough to unravel both.

blocks.tex: c_1 \oplus c_2 = (m_1 \oplus k) \oplus (m_2 \oplus k) = m_1 \oplus m_2
blocks.caption: The two-time pad. Every scheme that turns a key into a stream of bytes and XORs it (stream ciphers, and the CTR, GCM and ChaCha20 schemes of lessons 6 and 7) has this failure if a key is reused with the same nonce, the per-message value those schemes take.

blocks.code:
import secrets

def xor(a, b):
    return bytes(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))

m1, m2 = b"MEET9", b"RUN!!"

# Right: a fresh random key as long as the message, used once
k1 = secrets.token_bytes(len(m1))
c1 = xor(m1, k1)
assert xor(c1, k1) == m1

# Wrong: the same key for a second message (a "two-time pad")
k = bytes.fromhex("5a13c47e99")
c1, c2 = xor(m1, k), xor(m2, k)
print(xor(c1, c2).hex(" "))   # 1f 10 0b 75 18
print(xor(m1, m2).hex(" "))   # 1f 10 0b 75 18  the key cancelled out
blocks.caption: Runnable. secrets.token_bytes reads the operating system's secure random generator (lesson 12).

blocks.md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

blocks.question: Two ciphertexts were made with the same one-time pad. What can Eve compute without knowing the key?
options: Nothing: each ciphertext is perfectly secret
Only the lengths of the messages
The XOR of the two plaintexts
blocks.explain: XORing the ciphertexts cancels the key and leaves m1 XOR m2. From there, guessing likely words in one message reveals the other. The key itself only falls out once Eve also knows a plaintext.

blocks.question: Why does a one-time pad not replace AES for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic)?
options: Because XOR is too slow on modern CPUs
Because the key must be as long as all the traffic and delivered securely in advance
Because it was broken by quantum computers
Because it cannot encrypt binary data
blocks.explain: The pad is unbreakable but its key logistics are impossible at internet scale. Practical ciphers use a short key (16 or 32 bytes) and accept security based on computational difficulty.

lessons.title: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes

blocks.md:
A **block cipher** takes a fixed-size chunk of plaintext (a **block**) and a key, and outputs a ciphertext block of the same size. For a fixed key it is a reversible scramble, a **permutation**: every input block maps to exactly one output block and back. Without the key, the mapping should look like a randomly chosen permutation.

The block cipher everyone uses is **AES** (Advanced Encryption Standard), published by NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) as FIPS 197 (Federal Information Processing Standard 197). In 2000 NIST picked the **Rijndael** design by the cryptographers Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen as the winner of an open public competition.

What FIPS 197 fixes:

- Block size: always **128 bits** (16 bytes).
- Key size: 128, 192 or 256 bits, giving AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256.
- Rounds: the 16 bytes sit in a 4 x 4 grid called the **state**, and each round applies four steps. SubBytes swaps every byte through a fixed lookup table (the S-box), which breaks any simple algebraic pattern. ShiftRows rotates row r of the grid left by r places. MixColumns combines the four bytes of each column so each output byte depends on all four. AddRoundKey XORs in a round key derived from your key. After a few rounds every output bit depends on every input bit. AES-128 runs 10 rounds, AES-192 runs 12, AES-256 runs 14 (the last round skips MixColumns).

A 128-bit key has $2^{128} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ possible values. Trying them all is far beyond any computer that exists; attacks on AES in practice go after how it is used, not the cipher itself.

blocks.title: From a message to one AES block

scenes.caption: "HELLO WORLD" is 11 bytes (sp marks the space). AES only accepts exactly 16, so 5 positions are empty.
PKCS7 padding fills the gap: when N bytes are missing, append N bytes each holding the value N. Here N = 5, so five bytes of 05.
AES-128 with the FIPS 197 example key (00 01 02 ... 0f) turns the whole block into 16 unrelated-looking bytes (computed with the cryptography library).
Decrypting reverses the permutation, then the receiver reads the last byte (05), checks the five 05 bytes, and strips them.

blocks.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import padding

# One AES-128 block, using the test vector printed in FIPS 197 (Appendix C.1)
key = bytes.fromhex("000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f")
block = bytes.fromhex("00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff")
enc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB()).encryptor()
print(enc.update(block).hex())   # 69c4e0d86a7b0430d8cdb78070b4c55a

# Messages are rarely a multiple of 16 bytes: PKCS7 padding fills the gap
p = padding.PKCS7(128).padder()
print((p.update(b"HELLO WORLD") + p.finalize()).hex(" "))
# 48 45 4c 4c 4f 20 57 4f 52 4c 44 05 05 05 05 05  (5 bytes of value 5)
blocks.caption: Runnable. The first output matches the AES-128 example in FIPS 197 Appendix C.1, a good self-test for any AES implementation. `hazmat` is the library's "hazardous materials" layer of raw primitives.

blocks.md: Padding has a name worth decoding: **PKCS7** comes from PKCS #7, one of the Public-Key Cryptography Standards series that RSA Laboratories published. If a message is already a multiple of 16 bytes, a full extra block of sixteen `10` (hex for 16) bytes is added, so the receiver can always remove padding unambiguously.

A block cipher on its own encrypts exactly one block. Real messages are many blocks, and how you chain them (the **mode**) decides whether patterns leak. Calling raw AES block by block is the mistake of the next lesson.

blocks.question: How many bytes does AES encrypt in one call of the block function, whatever the key size?
blocks.explain: The AES block is always 128 bits, which is 16 bytes. Key size (128, 192 or 256 bits) only changes the key and the number of rounds.

blocks.question: A message is exactly 32 bytes long. How many bytes does it occupy after PKCS7 padding for AES?
blocks.explain: Already a multiple of 16, so a full block of padding (sixteen 0x10 bytes) is added: 48 bytes. This keeps unpadding unambiguous.

lessons.title: Modes of operation: why ECB leaks and what CBC and CTR fix

blocks.md:
A **mode of operation** is the rule for using a block cipher on many blocks. NIST SP 800-38A (Special Publication 800-38A) defines the classic ones.

**ECB** (Electronic Codebook) encrypts each block independently with the same key. The standard explains the name: like a codebook, it assigns "a fixed ciphertext block to each plaintext block". That is the problem. Equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks, so the **shape** of the data survives encryption.

blocks.title: An 8 x 8 image, one AES block per pixel

scenes.caption: Plaintext: a smiley face. Each cell is a 16-byte block of all FF (light) or all 00 (dark). Real images have many identical runs like this.
ECB with AES-128. Each cell shows the first ciphertext byte (computed). Only two values appear, 60 and 198, so the face is perfectly visible.
CBC with a random IV, same key. Every block depends on all the blocks before it, so equal pixels now encrypt differently and the picture is gone.

blocks.md:
This is the famous "ECB penguin": encrypt a bitmap of Tux, the Linux mascot, in ECB and the penguin is still recognisable. The fix is to make each block's encryption depend on something that changes.

**CBC** (Cipher Block Chaining) XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encrypting, so blocks are chained. The first block has no predecessor, so it is XORed with an **IV** (initialization vector): a fresh value per message that SP 800-38A says need not be secret but must be **unpredictable**.

**CTR** (Counter mode) never feeds the data through AES at all. It encrypts a counter (nonce, then 1, 2, 3, ...) to make a **keystream**, then XORs the keystream onto the data, like a one-time pad built from AES. SP 800-38A requires a **unique** counter block for every block ever encrypted under a key.

blocks.title: How CBC chains and CTR streams

scenes.caption: CBC, block 1: the random IV is XORed into P1, then AES encrypts it to give C1.
CBC, block 2: C1 is XORed into P2 before encryption. Change any earlier block (or the IV) and every later ciphertext block changes.
CTR: AES encrypts nonce plus counter, never the data. The output keystream is XORed onto the plaintext. Blocks are independent, so CTR runs in parallel.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Adobe, 2013.** In October 2013 Adobe disclosed a breach; KrebsOnSecurity reported it affected at least 38 million active users, and the leaked file held about 153 million records (Troy Hunt, who runs the breach service Have I Been Pwned, counted 152,989,508 that loaded cleanly). Adobe stated the system "used Triple DES encryption to protect all password information". Triple DES (3DES) is an older cipher built by applying DES, the Data Encryption Standard, three times. Password expert Steve Thomas pointed out it was used in **ECB** mode, and plain-text password **hints** sat beside each record.

The consequence: everyone with the same password got the same ciphertext. Jeremi Gosney, a password security expert, told Ars Technica that of 130 million encrypted passwords only 56 million were unique. [Troy Hunt showed](https://www.troyhunt.com/adobe-credentials-and-serious/) that grouping everyone who shared one ciphertext and reading all their hints gave many passwords away, without ever breaking 3DES.

blocks.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

key = os.urandom(32)
msg = b"YELLOW SUBMARINE" * 2          # two identical 16-byte blocks

# WRONG: ECB encrypts equal blocks to equal ciphertext
ecb = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB()).encryptor().update(msg)
print(ecb[:16] == ecb[16:])            # True: the pattern leaks

# Better: CBC with a fresh random IV; equal blocks now look unrelated
iv = os.urandom(16)
cbc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.CBC(iv)).encryptor().update(msg)
print(cbc[:16] == cbc[16:])            # False

# Still not done: neither mode detects tampering. Use AEAD (next lesson).
blocks.caption: Runnable. Wrong (ECB) next to better (CBC with a random IV). Passwords should not be encrypted at all; lesson 11 shows the right tool.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: forbid ECB in code review (search for `modes.ECB` and `AES/ECB` strings), and prefer an AEAD (next lesson). Detect: in stored ciphertext, count repeated 16-byte blocks; any repeats in non-trivial data mean ECB or a reused IV. Respond: re-encrypt with a correct mode and rotate keys.

blocks.question: Which property of ECB made the Adobe password file useful to attackers without decrypting anything?
options: Identical passwords produced identical ciphertexts, so users could be grouped and their hints pooled
The ciphertext was longer than the password
blocks.explain: ECB is deterministic per block. Grouping equal ciphertexts and reading all the hints for a group gave away common passwords, no key needed.

blocks.question: In CTR mode, what must never repeat under the same key?
blocks.explain: A repeated counter block repeats the keystream, which is the two-time pad from lesson 4. SP 800-38A requires every counter block under a key to be unique, across all messages.

lessons.title: Authenticated encryption: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and nonce reuse

blocks.md:
CBC and CTR give confidentiality only. Mallory cannot read the message but can still change it, and in CTR the change is surgical: flipping bit $i$ of the ciphertext flips exactly bit $i$ of the decrypted plaintext. NIST SP 800-38D calls this ciphertext **malleable** (it can be reshaped in a controlled way). If Mallory can guess the plaintext, Mallory can rewrite it.

CBC fails too, and worse. If a server answers "bad padding" differently from other errors, that one bit of feedback (a **padding oracle**) lets an attacker who resends altered ciphertexts decrypt them byte by byte. POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption), from Google researchers in 2014, used it to steal HTTPS cookies from SSL 3.0. Authentication checked before decryption removes the oracle.

blocks.title: Bit-flipping a CTR ciphertext (no key needed)

scenes.caption: Alice encrypts "PAY 100 TO BOB" with AES-256 in CTR mode. The keystream bytes are computed from a real key.
Ciphertext = plaintext XOR keystream. Mallory sees only this row.
Mallory knows the format and that byte 4 is the digit 1 (0x31). Mallory wants 9 (0x39). The difference is 0x08, so Mallory XORs 0x08 into ciphertext byte 4: 1b becomes 13.
Bob decrypts with the correct key and reads "PAY 900 TO BOB". Nothing failed; CTR has no way to notice.

blocks.md:
The fix is **AEAD** (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data), defined as an interface in RFC 5116 (an RFC, Request for Comments, is an Internet standard document). An AEAD encrypts **and** computes an authentication **tag** over the ciphertext. Decryption recomputes the tag and refuses to return anything if one bit changed. "Associated data" is extra data, such as a header or user id, that is authenticated but not encrypted, so it cannot be swapped.

Two AEADs dominate:

- **AES-GCM** (Galois/Counter Mode, NIST SP 800-38D): CTR-mode AES plus a tag computed with multiplication in a binary Galois field (a finite field, named after the mathematician Evariste Galois: arithmetic on 128-bit blocks that stays 128 bits). Very fast on CPUs with dedicated AES hardware.
- **ChaCha20-Poly1305** (RFC 8439): the ChaCha20 stream cipher, designed by Daniel J. Bernstein and named for its 20 rounds, plus the Poly1305 authenticator, which evaluates a polynomial modulo the prime $2^{130}-5$. RFC 8439 says it is about three times as fast as AES on platforms that lack specialised AES hardware.

blocks.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
aead = AESGCM(key)

nonce = os.urandom(12)                 # 96 bits, NEW for every message
header = b"user=42"                    # associated data: authenticated, not hidden
ct = aead.encrypt(nonce, b"PAY 100 TO BOB", header)
print(len(ct))                         # 30 = 14 bytes of text + 16-byte tag

print(aead.decrypt(nonce, ct, header)) # b'PAY 100 TO BOB'

tampered = bytearray(ct)
tampered[4] ^= 0x08                    # the CTR trick: turn '1' into '9'
try:
    aead.decrypt(nonce, bytes(tampered), header)
except InvalidTag:
    print("rejected: tag check failed")

try:
    aead.decrypt(nonce, ct, b"user=43") # header changed
except InvalidTag:
    print("rejected: associated data changed")
blocks.caption: Runnable. The same bit flip from the figure is now rejected. ChaCha20Poly1305 in the same library has an identical encrypt(nonce, data, associated_data) interface.

blocks.md:
Both take a **nonce**: a value that must never repeat for the same key. Both use 96-bit nonces. And both inherit the two-time pad weakness of their CTR-style core, with a worse twist. SP 800-38D Appendix A says that if a GCM nonce repeats, an attacker can likely recover the internal authentication key (the "hash subkey") and then forge valid tags for any ciphertext. RFC 5116 says nonce reuse "undermines all of the authenticity and integrity protection provided by that key".

**Real case: nonce-disrespecting servers, 2016.** Security researchers Hanno Böck, Aaron Zauner, Sean Devlin, Juraj Somorovsky and Philipp Jovanovic scanned the internet and found 184 HTTPS servers repeating AES-GCM nonces in TLS (Transport Layer Security, the protocol under HTTPS; lesson 16), including large corporations and a credit card company, and showed they could inject content into those encrypted sessions. They found over 70,000 more using random nonces, which risk collisions over long connections.

blocks.prompt: You pick each 96-bit GCM nonce at random. Roughly how many messages can you send under one key before NIST says to stop?
blocks.reveal: SP 800-38D caps random-nonce GCM at $2^{32}$ (about 4.3 billion) encryptions per key. The reason is the birthday effect from lesson 8: random 96-bit values start colliding with real probability long before $2^{96}$. High-volume systems use a counter nonce or rotate keys well before the cap.

blocks.md: Use an AEAD for every new design, generate a fresh nonce per message (a counter, or 12 random bytes with a usage limit), and treat a decrypt failure as an attack, never as "try again without checking".

Defender view. Prevent: one key per purpose, nonces from a counter or the OS random generator, key rotation before the limit. Detect: log and alert on authentication-tag failures (a burst means tampering or a bug); scan TLS endpoints for repeated nonces as Böck and colleagues did. Respond: rotate the key immediately; every message under a reused nonce pair must be considered forgeable.

blocks.question: A service encrypts with AES-GCM but uses a fixed nonce of 12 zero bytes for every message. What is lost?
options: Nothing, because GCM authenticates every message
Only the secrecy of the first message
Confidentiality of messages that share the nonce, and the ability to trust any tag under that key
blocks.explain: Repeated nonce means repeated keystream (plaintext XORs leak) and, per SP 800-38D Appendix A, likely recovery of the hash subkey, which lets an attacker forge tags. Both secrecy and integrity fail.

blocks.question: Why is the user id passed as associated data instead of being encrypted with the message?
options: The server needs to read it to route the message, but it must still be bound to the ciphertext so it cannot be swapped
Associated data makes the ciphertext shorter
It lets the server skip tag verification
blocks.explain: Associated data stays readable but is covered by the tag. Changing it (for example to another user's id) makes decryption fail, as the code shows.

lessons.title: Hash functions: fingerprints, avalanche and the birthday bound

blocks.md:
A **cryptographic hash function** maps any input (a password, a 4 GB disk image) to a fixed-size output called a **digest**. SHA-256 (from the SHA-2 family; SHA stands for Secure Hash Algorithm, standardised by NIST in FIPS 180-4) always outputs 256 bits. It has no key and is completely public. Same input, same digest, every time.

Three security properties, from weakest demand to strongest:

1. **Preimage resistance**: given a digest, you cannot find any input that produces it (one-way).
2. **Second-preimage resistance**: given an input, you cannot find a different input with the same digest.
3. **Collision resistance**: you cannot find **any** two different inputs with the same digest.

A good hash behaves as if its output were random. One visible symptom is the **avalanche effect**: change one input bit and about half of the output bits flip, with no pattern. The digits 1 and 9 in ASCII are `00110001` and `00111001`, a single bit apart. Watch what that does to SHA-256.

blocks.title: One input bit changed, half the output changed

scenes.caption: First 8 of the 32 digest bytes of SHA-256("pay 100"), computed with hashlib.
SHA-256("pay 900"): the inputs differ in one bit, yet the digests share no visible structure.
Bits differing per byte (out of 8): 7, 2, 5, 4, 5, 2, 5, 4. Over all 256 bits, exactly 128 differ for this pair: half, as an ideal random function predicts.

blocks.title: Output bits flipped by a 1-bit input change (SHA-256)

scenes.caption: Each pair of inputs differs in exactly one bit. Computed: 125, 122 and 128 of 256 output bits flip, scattered around the ideal 128.

blocks.code:
import hashlib

def bits_different(a: bytes, b: bytes) -> int:
    return sum(bin(x ^ y).count("1") for x, y in zip(a, b))

h1 = hashlib.sha256(b"pay 100").digest()
h2 = hashlib.sha256(b"pay 900").digest()   # '1' and '9' differ in 1 bit
print(h1.hex()[:16])                     # 00ee27a7cebbb049
print(h2.hex()[:16])                     # bfccbad52beb7ec7
print(bits_different(h1, h2), "of 256")  # 128 of 256
blocks.caption: Runnable. hashlib ships with Python; digest() gives raw bytes, hexdigest() gives hex text.

blocks.md: **The birthday bound.** In a room of 23 people, two probably share a birthday, far fewer than 365. The same maths says that for an $n$-bit hash you expect a collision after about $2^{n/2}$ random inputs, not $2^n$. So a 128-bit digest gives only about 64 bits of collision resistance, and SHA-256 gives about 128. This is why digests are long.

blocks.title: Chance of any collision vs number of hashes computed

scenes.caption: n = 128 (MD5's digest size): collisions become likely near 2^64 hashes, not 2^128.
n = 64: about 2^32 (4 billion) hashes, an afternoon on one machine. Short digests or tags are collision-prone.
n = 256 (SHA-256): you need about 2^128 hashes, far beyond reach. Standard approximation, k = 2^x random inputs.

blocks.question: Which property must a hash have so that nobody can create two different contracts with the same digest, one innocent and one malicious?
blocks.explain: The attacker controls both documents, so they only need any pair that collides: that is collision resistance, the property MD5 and SHA-1 lost (next lesson).

blocks.question: Roughly how many random inputs until a collision is likely for a 160-bit hash such as SHA-1, if the hash were ideal?
blocks.explain: Birthday bound: about 2^(n/2) = 2^80. Real attacks on SHA-1 do better than that by exploiting its structure.

lessons.title: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision

blocks.md:
**MD5** (Message-Digest algorithm 5) was published by Ron Rivest in RFC 1321 in April 1992 as an extension of the earlier MD4, with a 128-bit digest. RFC 6151 records its decline: the first collisions for full MD5 were published in 2004, detailed techniques in 2005, and later work found collisions within seconds. RFC 6151 concludes MD5 "is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required such as digital signatures".

Why do collisions matter so much for signatures? A digital signature (lesson 15) signs the **hash** of a document, not the document. If two documents share a hash, a signature on one is valid on the other. The key example is a **certificate**: a signed statement binding a name to a public key, issued by a **CA** (certificate authority), an organisation whose signatures operating systems and browsers trust.

**Real case: Flame, 2012.** Flame was espionage malware found in May 2012 by Iran's national CERT (computer emergency response team), the security company Kaspersky Lab and the Hungarian university lab CrySyS, with most infections in Iran. It spread inside networks by posing as a Windows Update package, signed by a certificate that chained to Microsoft.

How it got that certificate: Microsoft's Terminal Server Licensing Service still issued certificates signed with **MD5**. Marc Stevens, a cryptanalyst at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science), analysed the forged certificate and found a **chosen-prefix collision**: the attackers prepared an innocent-looking certificate request and a malicious code-signing certificate whose signed parts had the same MD5 hash, so Microsoft's signature on the first was valid on the second. Stevens found the collision method was a previously unknown variant, which pointed to world-class cryptanalysis behind the malware.

blocks.title: How an MD5 collision turned into a trusted signature

scenes.caption: A legitimate chain: Windows trusts the Microsoft root, which trusts the licensing CA.
The attacker gets an ordinary-looking certificate signed by the licensing CA, which hashes it with MD5 and signs the hash.
The attacker had crafted a second certificate, with code-signing powers, whose signed part has the same MD5 digest.
So the CA's signature on A verifies on B as well. B signs Flame, which Windows accepts as a genuine Microsoft update.

blocks.md:
Microsoft responded with Security Advisory 2718704 on 3 June 2012, revoking trust in the affected intermediate certificates on all supported Windows versions.

**Real case: SHAttered, 2017.** SHA-1 (160-bit digest) was the successor many systems moved to. On 23 February 2017 researchers from CWI Amsterdam and Google, including Marc Stevens and Elie Bursztein, announced the first SHA-1 collision: two different PDF files with the same SHA-1 hash. It took about 9,223,372,036,854,775,808 SHA-1 computations: 6,500 CPU-years (years of one ordinary processor) for the first phase and 110 GPU-years (graphics processors, which run thousands of simple calculations in parallel) for the second. Google's Chrome team had already announced a phase-out of SHA-1 certificates in 2014, and NIST has said SHA-1 must be phased out entirely by 31 December 2030.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, hmac

data = b"installer bytes ..."     # the file you downloaded
published = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()   # what the vendor printed

# WRONG: MD5 or SHA-1 for anything an attacker can prepare in advance
weak = hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()

# RIGHT: SHA-256 (or SHA-3); compare_digest is harmless here, but constant time only matters for secret values such as MAC tags (lesson 10)
ok = hmac.compare_digest(hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest(), published)
print(ok)                          # True

# A hash only proves the file matches the hash you were given.
# If the attacker can change the web page that shows the hash too,
# you need a signature (lesson 15), not just a hash.
blocks.caption: Runnable. Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for anything an attacker could prepare in advance; MD5 and SHA-1 survive only in places that need no collision resistance.

blocks.md: "It is only a checksum" is how MD5 and SHA-1 linger. Any place where an attacker can choose the input that gets hashed (certificates, signed documents, deduplication, commit ids, package lockfiles) needs collision resistance.

Defender view. Prevent: ban MD5 and SHA-1 for signatures, certificates and integrity checks (configure CAs, signing tools and TLS libraries to refuse them). Detect: Stevens' counter-cryptanalysis checks a single file or certificate for the traces a collision attack leaves; it took 0.03 seconds to flag Flame's certificate. Respond: revoke anything signed with the broken hash, as Microsoft did, and re-sign with SHA-256.

blocks.question: Why could Flame's authors reuse Microsoft's signature instead of forging one?
options: The signature covered an MD5 hash, and their malicious certificate had the same MD5 hash as one Microsoft did sign
blocks.explain: Signatures sign hashes. A collision means two different inputs share the hash, so one signature validates both. No key was stolen.

blocks.question: A team stores SHA-1 hashes of uploaded files to detect duplicates and auto-merge "identical" uploads from different users. What is the risk?
options: None, SHA-1 is only weak for passwords
SHA-1 hashes are too long to store
An attacker can upload a harmless file and a harmful one with the same SHA-1, and the system will treat them as the same file
blocks.explain: Users choose the inputs, so collision resistance is needed. SHAttered showed two different PDFs with one SHA-1. Use SHA-256.

lessons.title: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key

blocks.md:
A hash proves nothing about **who** made it: anyone can compute SHA-256 of a modified message. To get integrity and authenticity between two parties who share a secret key, use a **MAC** (message authentication code): a short tag computed from the key and the message. The receiver recomputes the tag with the same key and compares. Without the key, Mallory cannot produce a valid tag for a changed message.

The obvious home-made MAC is `hash(key + message)`. With MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 this is broken by a **length-extension attack**.

Why: these hashes are built in the Merkle-Damgård style (named after Ralph Merkle and Ivan Damgård, who independently proved the design sound), processing the input block by block and carrying an internal **state**. The final digest **is** that state. So a digest of `key + message` lets anyone resume hashing where it stopped and append more data, getting a valid digest of `key + message + padding + extra` without knowing the key.

**Real case: Flickr API, 2009.** Security researchers Thai Duong and Juliano Rizzo showed that Flickr signed API requests as MD5(secret + parameters). Because MD5 allows length extension, they could append parameters to a signed request and compute a valid signature without the secret, forging requests on behalf of any Flickr application. SHA-3 (FIPS 202) was designed to resist length extension, but the standard fix for any hash is HMAC.

blocks.title: Length extension against hash(key + message)

scenes.caption: The server publishes tag = SHA-256(key + message). The hash ends in its internal state, and the tag is exactly that state.
The attacker loads the tag as the starting state and keeps hashing extra blocks. The key is never needed: it is already folded into the state.
HMAC stops this: the outer hash is keyed again, so a state taken from the output cannot be continued into a valid tag.

blocks.md: **HMAC** (keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code, RFC 2104 by Hugo Krawczyk, Mihir Bellare and Ran Canetti) wraps any hash twice with two fixed masks, `ipad` (inner pad: the byte 0x36 repeated) and `opad` (outer pad: 0x5C repeated):

blocks.caption: || means concatenation (joining bytes). The inner hash processes the message; the outer hash, keyed again, hides the inner state, which blocks length extension.

blocks.md: The second classic MAC bug is in **checking** the tag. A normal string comparison stops at the first different byte. A tag with a correct first byte takes slightly longer to reject than one with a wrong first byte. An attacker who can measure that time can guess the tag byte by byte, instead of all at once. The fix is a **constant-time comparison**, which always looks at every byte. Python's `hmac.compare_digest` documents exactly this: it avoids "content-based short circuiting behaviour".

blocks.title: Why == leaks timing

scenes.caption: Expected tag 7f3a, attacker's guess 00..: compared at i = 0 and rejected after one step.
Guess 7f.. with the first byte right: one more loop iteration before rejection. That extra time tells the attacker byte 0 is correct.

Repeat per byte: about 256 guesses per byte instead of 256 to the power of the tag length. Once every byte matches the loop finishes and returns True. compare_digest removes the early exit so time does not depend on where bytes differ.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, hmac, secrets

key = secrets.token_bytes(32)
msg = b"amount=100&to=bob"

# WRONG 1: hash(secret + message) is open to length extension
bad_tag = hashlib.sha256(key + msg).hexdigest()

# RIGHT: HMAC, the construction from RFC 2104
tag = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def verify(key, msg, received_tag):
    expected = hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    # WRONG 2: expected == received_tag stops at the first different
    # character, so its timing leaks how much of the tag was right.
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, received_tag)   # RIGHT

print(verify(key, msg, tag))                      # True
print(verify(key, b"amount=900&to=bob", tag))     # False
blocks.caption: Runnable. Two wrongs, both fixed with the standard library.

blocks.md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

Defender view. Prevent: HMAC-SHA-256 or an AEAD, hmac.compare_digest, and a timestamp inside the signed data so old messages cannot be replayed. Detect: log tag failures per client; many failures from one source mean probing or a misconfigured key. Respond: rotate the shared key, which makes every tag the attacker collected useless.

blocks.question: Why does HMAC resist length extension while SHA-256(key + message) does not?
options: HMAC's output comes from a second, keyed hash, so the published value is not a state anyone can continue
blocks.explain: In the naive design the tag is the final state of a hash over attacker-extendable input. HMAC's outer keyed hash means the tag is not a resumable state of the inner computation.

blocks.question: A webhook handler checks `if request_sig == expected_sig:`. What is the risk, and the fix?
options: Timing side channel; compare with hmac.compare_digest
blocks.explain: String == exits at the first mismatch, leaking how many leading bytes match through response time. hmac.compare_digest compares in time that does not depend on the content.

lessons.title: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose

blocks.md:
A password database will eventually be stolen; plan for it. The attacker then guesses passwords offline, hashing each guess and comparing. Two features of a plain SHA-256 make this easy: it is **fast** (built to hash gigabytes per second), and with no **salt** (a random per-user value mixed in) two users with the same password have the same hash, so one guess tests everyone at once, and precomputed tables work.

A **password hashing function** is the opposite of a fast hash: deliberately slow, salted, and ideally **memory-hard** (needing lots of RAM per guess, which hurts attackers using GPUs).

The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit foundation that publishes free application security guidance) currently recommends, in order:

- **Argon2id** with at least 19 MiB (mebibytes, 1,048,576 bytes each) of memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism. Argon2 is a memory-hard function specified in RFC 9106; Argon2id is its recommended variant.
- **scrypt** (a memory-hard password function by Colin Percival, RFC 7914) with a cost of $2^{17}$, block size 8, parallelism 1, if Argon2id is not available.
- **bcrypt** (a 1999 password hash by Niels Provos and David Mazières, built on the Blowfish cipher) with a work factor of 10 or more, for legacy systems (note its 72-byte input limit).
- **PBKDF2** (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2, RFC 8018) with HMAC-SHA-256 and 600,000 or more iterations when FIPS 140 (US certified crypto modules) compliance is required.

The companion course *Authentication and identity attacks* covers storage, cracking and credential stuffing in depth.

blocks.title: Time to try N guesses: fast hash vs slow hash (model)

scenes.caption: Model with assumed costs: hours = guesses x ms per guess / 3.6 million. A fast hash at 1 ns per guess clears a billion guesses in about one second.
A slow hash tuned to 100 ms per guess makes the same billion guesses take over 27,000 hours on one machine. You pay 100 ms once per login; the attacker pays it per guess.

Raise the cost to 1 s and the attacker's time grows tenfold again: a billion guesses now take over 277,000 hours. Real cracking rigs run many machines in parallel, which is why memory-hard settings matter too.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, hmac, os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF

password = b"correct horse"

# WRONG: one fast, unsalted hash; equal passwords give equal hashes
weak = hashlib.sha256(password).hexdigest()

# RIGHT: a slow, salted password hash (scrypt, OWASP minimum settings)
salt = os.urandom(16)
stored = hashlib.scrypt(password, salt=salt, n=2**17, r=8, p=1,
                        maxmem=2**28, dklen=32)

def check(attempt: bytes) -> bool:
    h = hashlib.scrypt(attempt, salt=salt, n=2**17, r=8, p=1,
                       maxmem=2**28, dklen=32)
    return hmac.compare_digest(h, stored)

print(check(b"correct horse"), check(b"Correct horse"))   # True False

# Different job: turn one strong shared secret into separate keys (HKDF)
shared = os.urandom(32)
def subkey(label: bytes) -> bytes:
    return HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32,
                salt=None, info=label).derive(shared)
print(subkey(b"client to server") != subkey(b"server to client"))  # True
blocks.caption: Runnable (scrypt with the OWASP minimum takes a noticeable fraction of a second, which is the point). hashlib.scrypt needs maxmem raised because n=2^17, r=8 uses 128 MiB.

blocks.md: **Key derivation** is a different job with a similar name. A **KDF** (key derivation function) turns some secret input into one or more keys of the right size. Password KDFs (Argon2, scrypt, PBKDF2) stretch weak human secrets. When the input is already strong, for example the shared secret from a Diffie-Hellman exchange (lesson 13), you use a fast KDF such as **HKDF** (HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function, RFC 5869). It first **extracts** the randomness into a fixed-size key with HMAC, then **expands** it into as many separate keys as you need, each tied to a label so keys for different purposes never coincide. TLS 1.3 builds its whole key schedule from HKDF.
Do not use one key for two jobs (say, encryption and MAC, or client-to-server and server-to-client). Derive separate keys with HKDF and distinct labels.

Defender view. Prevent: Argon2id or scrypt with a unique salt; upgrade legacy fast hashes by rehashing at each user's next login. Detect: alert on bulk reads of the credentials table and on login spikes that follow a leak. Respond: force password resets, invalidate sessions and tell users who reused the password elsewhere.

blocks.question: Why is a per-user random salt essential even with a slow hash?
options: It makes each hash faster to verify
It replaces the need for a slow hash
Without it, users with the same password share a hash, so one guess tests all of them and precomputed tables work
blocks.explain: Salts make every user's hash unique, forcing the attacker to attack each account separately and defeating precomputation. Slowness then multiplies the cost of each separate attack.

blocks.question: You have a 32-byte random shared secret from a key exchange and need an encryption key and a MAC key. Which tool fits?
options: HKDF with two different info labels
SHA-1 of the secret, split in half
Use the secret directly for both
blocks.explain: The input is already high-entropy, so no stretching is needed. HKDF extracts and expands it into independent keys per label.

lessons.title: Randomness: where keys come from, and the Debian disaster

blocks.md:
Every key, IV, nonce and salt in this course must be **unpredictable**. Computers are deterministic, so they use a **PRNG** (pseudorandom number generator): an algorithm that expands a starting value, the **seed**, into a long sequence that looks random. The word "pseudo" is honest: the same seed always gives the same sequence.

A **CSPRNG** (cryptographically secure PRNG) adds a guarantee: even after seeing lots of output, nobody can predict the next bit or recover earlier ones, **provided the seed has enough entropy**. Entropy is a measure of unpredictability, counted in bits: a fair coin flip is 1 bit. The operating system gathers entropy from hardware events and serves it through a CSPRNG (on Linux the file `/dev/urandom` or the `getrandom` system call, on Windows the `BCryptGenRandom` function).

Python makes the difference explicit. The `random` module uses the Mersenne Twister (a PRNG whose sequence repeats only after $2^{19937}-1$ outputs, a Mersenne prime), and its documentation says it is "completely unsuitable for cryptographic purposes". It is predictable by design, and if you seed it with the time, an attacker only has to try the plausible times. The `secrets` module reads the operating system's best source, and its docs suggest 32 bytes (256 bits) of randomness for tokens.

blocks.title: A time-seeded token can be rebuilt
blocks.code:
import random, time
random.seed(int(time.time()))
token = '%032x' % random.getrandbits(128)

# attacker, later:
t = int(time.time())          # roughly when it happened
for guess in range(t - 5, t + 1):
    random.seed(guess)
    if '%032x' % random.getrandbits(128) == token:
        print('rebuilt from seed', guess)

scenes.caption: The server seeds Mersenne Twister with the current second. The token looks like 128 random bits.
The real uncertainty is only which second it was. An attacker who knows it was the last few seconds has a handful of seeds to try, not 2^128.
Each guess reseeds and regenerates. One matches, and the token is rebuilt. secrets.token_urlsafe(32) has no seed to guess.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Debian OpenSSL, CVE-2008-0166.** (A CVE, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry, is the public id for a known vulnerability.) In 2006 a Debian maintainer looked at warnings from Valgrind, a memory-checking tool, about OpenSSL reading uninitialised memory in its random generator. They asked on the openssl-dev mailing list whether two `MD_Update` lines (calls that feed data into the generator's entropy pool) could be removed, and got replies that it seemed fine. One line was harmless to remove; the other was the call that mixed **all** real entropy into the pool.

From September 2006 until the researcher Luciano Bello noticed in May 2008, Debian and derived systems like Ubuntu seeded OpenSSL with little more than the **process ID** (PID), which by default only goes up to 32,767. Russ Cox's analysis puts it plainly: ssh-keygen "could only generate 32,767 different possible SSH keys of a given type and size". Anyone could generate all of them and match public keys found on servers.

blocks.title: Bits of unpredictability in a generated key

scenes.caption: Debian keys had about 15 bits of uncertainty (log2 of 32,767 is 15.0): one laptop can generate every possible key.
A key from a healthy CSPRNG has its full 128 or 256 bits. Note the bars are bits, so each extra bit doubles the work: 128 bits is 2^113 times harder than 15.

blocks.code:
import random, secrets, time

# WRONG: Python's random module, seeded with the time
random.seed(int(time.time()))
weak_token = "%032x" % random.getrandbits(128)

# Anyone who can guess the second you did it can rebuild the token:
t = int(time.time())
for guess in range(t - 5, t + 1):
    random.seed(guess)
    if "%032x" % random.getrandbits(128) == weak_token:
        print("token rebuilt from seed", guess)

# RIGHT: the secrets module reads the operating system's CSPRNG
print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))     # 32 random bytes, URL-safe text
print(secrets.token_bytes(16).hex()) # e.g. a 128-bit key or nonce
blocks.caption: Runnable. The first half shows the flaw on your own process; the second half is the fix to use everywhere.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: generate secrets with the OS CSPRNG (Python's secrets or os.urandom, Java's SecureRandom) and never patch crypto code without its owners' review. Detect: [UC San Diego researchers](https://hovav.net/ucsd/dist/debiankey.pdf) scanned over 50,000 servers daily and found 751 with weak certificates; 30% were still weak six months later. Respond: Ubuntu's advisory said all keys made on affected systems "must be considered untrustworthy": regenerate them and revoke certificates.
A random-looking output says nothing about its entropy. Debian's weak keys passed every visual check; their weakness was only visible by counting how many could exist.

blocks.question: Why did Debian's broken generator still produce different keys on different runs, hiding the bug for almost two years?
options: The kernel added entropy later anyway
OpenSSL used the time of day
The process ID was still mixed in, giving about 32,767 variants
blocks.explain: Russ Cox notes the PID kept the output from being completely deterministic. If every key had been identical, the bug would likely have been caught quickly.

blocks.question: Which Python call should generate a password-reset token?
blocks.explain: secrets reads the OS CSPRNG. random is predictable from its state or seed, uuid1 encodes time and the machine address, and hashing the time adds no entropy.

lessons.title: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public

blocks.md:
Everything so far assumed Alice and Bob already share a key. How do two strangers on the internet get one, when Eve sees every byte? In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, then at Stanford University, published "New Directions in Cryptography" with an answer now called the **Diffie-Hellman key exchange** (DH, named after them).

It rests on a one-way property of modular arithmetic (from lesson 2). Fix a prime $p$ and a number $g$. Computing $g^a \bmod p$ is fast even for huge numbers. But given the result, finding $a$ (the **discrete logarithm**) is believed to be infeasible when $p$ is large enough. Exponentiation scrambles, and there is no shortcut back.

blocks.title: Powers of 5 mod 23 jump around

scenes.caption: Each value is the previous one times 5, then mod 23 (computed). Going forward is just multiplication.
The outputs visit every number 1 to 22 once in a scrambled order, so 5 is a generator mod 23. Given 8, which x? You scan the table: x = 6.
With 23 there are only 22 entries to scan. Real DH uses primes of 2048 bits or more (or elliptic curves), where the best known algorithms, far smarter than scanning, are still infeasible.

blocks.title: Diffie-Hellman with p = 23, g = 5

scenes.caption: Public setup: everyone, including Eve, knows p = 23 and g = 5. Alice secretly picks a = 6, Bob picks b = 15.
Alice sends A = 5^6 mod 23 = 8. Eve records it.
Bob sends B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19. Eve records that too.
Alice computes 19^6 mod 23 = 2. Bob computes 8^15 mod 23 = 2. Both get 2 = 5^(6 x 15) mod 23. Eve has 8 and 19 but would need a or b.
Bob's view of the same result. Neither secret exponent ever crossed the wire; only g^a and g^b did.

blocks.caption: Why both sides agree. Eve sees g^a and g^b; getting g^ab from those is the Diffie-Hellman problem, believed hard for large p.

blocks.md:
**The catch: DH alone has no authentication.** Alice cannot tell whether 19 came from Bob or from Mallory. Mallory can sit in the middle (a **man-in-the-middle** attack), run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob, and relay everything while reading it. With our numbers and Mallory's secret m = 9: Mallory sends 5^9 mod 23 = 11 to both, shares 9 with Alice and 10 with Bob, and re-encrypts between them.

That is why real protocols **sign** the exchange (lessons 14 and 15): in TLS the server signs the handshake with the key in its certificate. DH gives a shared secret; signatures prove who you share it with.

blocks.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey

# Toy Diffie-Hellman with school-sized numbers (never use these sizes)
p, g = 23, 5
a, b = 6, 15                  # Alice's and Bob's secrets
A, B = pow(g, a, p), pow(g, b, p)
print(A, B)                   # 8 19   (sent in the open)
print(pow(B, a, p), pow(A, b, p))   # 2 2   (same shared secret)

# Real code: X25519, an elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman
alice, bob = X25519PrivateKey.generate(), X25519PrivateKey.generate()
s1 = alice.exchange(bob.public_key())
s2 = bob.exchange(alice.public_key())
print(s1 == s2, len(s1))      # True 32
# Next: feed s1 into HKDF to get keys, and authenticate the public keys.
blocks.caption: Runnable. The toy numbers, then X25519, a Diffie-Hellman on the elliptic curve Curve25519 (RFC 7748) that works modulo the prime 2^255 - 19.

blocks.md: Defender view. Weak DH groups are a real failure: the 2015 [Logjam](https://weakdh.org/) research showed a man in the middle could downgrade TLS to 512-bit export-grade DH (deliberately weak settings from 1990s US export rules), then break it using a precomputation against the most common 512-bit prime. Prevent: allow only X25519 or 2048-bit-plus groups, and never unauthenticated DH. Detect: TLS scanners report DH group sizes; alert on anything below 2048 bits.

blocks.question: Eve recorded p = 23, g = 5, A = 8 and B = 19. What does Eve still lack to compute the shared secret directly?
options: Either secret exponent a or b (a discrete log)
Nothing, the secret is A x B mod p
blocks.explain: The shared secret is g^(ab). From public values alone Eve needs a discrete log; at 23 that is a table lookup, at 2048 bits it is infeasible.

blocks.question: Why does TLS sign the Diffie-Hellman values instead of just exchanging them?
options: Plain DH cannot tell Bob from a man in the middle; the signature proves the server's identity
DH values are too short without a signature
blocks.explain: DH guarantees a shared secret with whoever answered. Authentication (certificate plus signature) ensures that whoever answered is the real server.

lessons.title: RSA with tiny numbers: encryption, signing and padding

blocks.md:
DH agrees on a key; **public-key encryption** lets anyone encrypt to you using a key you publish. **RSA**, named after Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, who published it in 1978 in "A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems", is the classic scheme. You get a pair of keys: a **public key** you hand to the world and a **private key** you never share.

Its one-way function: multiplying two large primes is easy, but factoring the product back into those primes is believed infeasible at sizes like 3072 bits.

Key generation with toy numbers:

1. Pick primes $p = 61$, $q = 53$. Then $n = pq = 3233$ (public).
2. Compute $\varphi = (p-1)(q-1) = 3120$. Only someone who knows $p$ and $q$ can do this easily.
3. Pick a public exponent $e = 17$ that shares no factor with 3120.
4. Find the private exponent $d$ with $ed \bmod \varphi = 1$: $d = 2753$ (found with the extended Euclidean algorithm, which Python's `pow(e, -1, phi)` runs; check: 17 x 2753 = 46801 = 15 x 3120 + 1).

Public key: $(n, e) = (3233, 17)$. Private key: $d = 2753$.

blocks.tex: c = m^{e} \bmod n \qquad m = c^{d} \bmod n \qquad\quad 65^{17} \bmod 3233 = 2790,\;\; 2790^{2753} \bmod 3233 = 65
blocks.caption: Encrypt with the public exponent, decrypt with the private one (all values computed with Python's pow).

blocks.title: Textbook RSA, step by step
blocks.code:
p, q, e = 61, 53, 17
n = p * q
phi = (p - 1) * (q - 1)
d = pow(e, -1, phi)
c = pow(65, e, n)
m = pow(c, d, n)
sig = pow(123, d, n)
ok = pow(sig, e, n) == 123

scenes.caption: n is public; the primes stay secret.
phi needs p and q. pow(e, -1, phi) finds d with e x d = 1 mod phi.
Anyone encrypts 65 with the public key (e, n).
Only the holder of d gets 65 back.
Signing runs it the other way: raise a hash value (here 123) to the private d. Anyone checks with the public e.

blocks.md:
**Why "textbook RSA" is insecure.** The raw formula above is deterministic and malleable. Deterministic: 65 always encrypts to 2790, so Eve can test guesses ("is the answer yes or no?") by encrypting them with the public key. Malleable: multiplying the ciphertext by $2^e$ gives a valid encryption of $2m$ (here 3017 decrypts to 130), with no key.

Real RSA always adds **padding** with randomness and structure, defined in PKCS #1 (RFC 8017):

- **OAEP** (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) for encryption.
- **PSS** (Probabilistic Signature Scheme) for signatures.

The older PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption padding is the target of padding oracle attacks, first shown by Daniel Bleichenbacher: a server that reveals whether decrypted padding was valid lets an attacker decrypt step by step. The 2016 [DROWN attack](https://drownattack.com/) (Decrypting RSA with Obsolete and Weakened eNcryption) used one to decrypt TLS connections. In practice RSA encrypts only short secrets such as a symmetric key; the data itself goes through an AEAD.

blocks.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding

# Textbook RSA with tiny primes (insecure: for seeing the arithmetic only)
p, q, e = 61, 53, 17
n, phi = p * q, (p - 1) * (q - 1)      # 3233, 3120
d = pow(e, -1, phi)                    # 2753
c = pow(65, e, n)
print(c, pow(c, d, n))                 # 2790 65

# Real code: 3072-bit key, OAEP padding for encryption
key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=3072)
oaep = padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()),
                    algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)
ct = key.public_key().encrypt(b"session key bytes", oaep)
print(key.decrypt(ct, oaep))           # b'session key bytes'

# and PSS padding for signatures
pss = padding.PSS(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()),
                  salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH)
sig = key.sign(b"release-1.2.tar.gz", pss, hashes.SHA256())
key.public_key().verify(sig, b"release-1.2.tar.gz", pss, hashes.SHA256())
print("signature ok")                  # verify raises if it is not
blocks.caption: Runnable. Toy arithmetic first, then the real API: 3072-bit key, OAEP for encryption, PSS for signatures.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: RSA keys of at least 2048 bits, OAEP and PSS only, no SSLv2 (an obsolete predecessor of TLS) anywhere the key is used. Plan the move off RSA: NIST will deprecate it, with all quantum-vulnerable public-key crypto, after 2030 (NIST IR 8547). Detect: TLS scanners report key sizes, padding and legacy protocols. Respond: if a private key may be exposed, revoke its certificate and issue a new key.

If you ever write pow(m, e, n) in production code you have built textbook RSA. Call a library's OAEP or PSS function, or better, avoid RSA encryption entirely and use an elliptic-curve key exchange plus an AEAD.

blocks.question: Why must RSA encryption be randomised (OAEP) rather than computed as m^e mod n?
options: Without randomness, equal messages give equal ciphertexts, so an attacker can confirm guesses by encrypting them with the public key
Because n must change every message
blocks.explain: The public key is public, so anyone can encrypt candidate plaintexts and compare. Randomised padding makes each encryption different.

blocks.question: What does an attacker actually need to compute the private exponent d from the public key (n, e)?
options: Nothing more: d can be computed from e alone
The prime factors p and q of n, because phi = (p-1)(q-1) needs them
blocks.explain: phi needs the factors of n, and d is the inverse of e mod phi. For n = 3233 the factors 61 and 53 are found instantly, so the toy key is broken; factoring a 3072-bit n is believed infeasible, and that is RSA's whole security.

lessons.title: Elliptic curves and digital signatures: the PS3 and CurveBall

blocks.md:
A **digital signature** is the public-key version of a MAC. The signer uses a private key; anyone with the matching public key can verify. Unlike a MAC, verifiers cannot sign, so a signature proves **who** signed to everyone (and the signer cannot later deny it). Signatures protect software updates, certificates, Git tags and TLS handshakes.

Modern signatures mostly use **elliptic curves**. An elliptic curve here is the set of points $(x, y)$ satisfying $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$, with all arithmetic done mod a prime. There is a rule for "adding" two points to get a third, and adding a point $G$ to itself $k$ times gives $kG$. Computing $kG$ is fast; recovering $k$ from $kG$ is the elliptic-curve discrete log, believed infeasible on real curves. That gives the same one-way trap as DH, with much smaller keys.

blocks.title: Multiples of G = (5,1) on y^2 = x^3 + 2x + 2 mod 17

scenes.caption: A toy curve with 18 points plus a special "point at infinity" (inf). Each entry is G added to the previous one (computed).
A private key is a number d; the public key is dG. With d = 7, the public key is (0,6). Going from 7 to (0,6) is easy; from (0,6) back to 7 means searching.
At k = 19 we reach infinity and the cycle restarts: the group order is n = 19. Real curves have far more: about 2^256 points for P-256 (a NIST curve) and 2^255 for Curve25519.

blocks.md: **ECDSA** (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, NIST FIPS 186-5) signs a message hash $z$ with private key $d$. For every signature it picks a fresh secret number $k$, which FIPS 186-5 calls the **per-message secret number** (often called the nonce), and outputs the pair $(r, s)$:

blocks.tex: r = x\text{-coordinate of } kG \bmod n, \qquad s = k^{-1}(z + r\,d) \bmod n
blocks.caption: k must be secret and different for every signature. FIPS 186-5 says a pre-computed k must be protected like the private key itself.

blocks.md:
**Real case: Sony PlayStation 3, 2010.** Sony signed PS3 software with ECDSA so the console would only run Sony-approved code. On 29 December 2010, at the 27th Chaos Communication Congress (27C3, an annual hacker conference in Germany), the console-hacking group fail0verflow showed that Sony used the **same** $k$ for every signature. Their slide of "Sony's ECDSA code" was a joke function that always returns 4.

With a repeated $k$, two signatures share $r$, and two equations in two unknowns give up everything. Toy numbers on our curve: $d = 7$, $k = 10$, hashes $z_1 = 5$ and $z_2 = 12$ give signatures $(7, 13)$ and $(7, 8)$.

blocks.tex: k = \frac{z_1 - z_2}{s_1 - s_2} = \frac{5 - 12}{13 - 8} \equiv 10, \qquad d = \frac{s_1 k - z_1}{r} = \frac{13 \cdot 10 - 5}{7} \equiv 7 \pmod{19}
blocks.caption: Division here means multiplying by the inverse mod 19. Same algebra as fail0verflow's slide (which calls the per-signature number m and the private key k): with Sony's private key known, anyone could sign code the console would trust.

blocks.md: **The fix is to remove the random number.** **Deterministic** signatures derive $k$ from the private key and the message. RFC 6979 does this for ECDSA, FIPS 186-5 includes deterministic ECDSA, and **Ed25519** (EdDSA, the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm of RFC 8032) is deterministic by design. RFC 8032 notes this "protects against attacks" from poor randomness. Different messages get different $k$; the same message gets the same signature, which is harmless.

**Real case: CurveBall, CVE-2020-0601.** In January 2020 Microsoft patched a flaw that the US NSA (National Security Agency) reported in `crypt32.dll`, the Windows CryptoAPI library that validates certificates. Ben Perez of the security firm Trail of Bits explained it: Windows matched a certificate's root by its **public key** but accepted custom curve parameters, including the generator $G$. An attacker could take a trusted root's public key $Q$, pick their own private key $d'$, and declare a generator $G' = d'^{-1} Q$. Then $d' G' = Q$: the attacker "owns" a trusted root's public key on a curve of their choosing, with no maths broken.

blocks.title: CurveBall: trusting a key without its curve

nodes.label:
Trusted root store
key Q on P-256

Attacker root
same Q, own G'

scenes.caption: Windows keeps trusted roots. Each is a public key Q on a standard curve with a standard generator G.
The attacker builds a root certificate with the same Q but explicit curve parameters, choosing G' so that their own d' satisfies d'G' = Q.
The vulnerable check compared only Q, not the curve parameters, so the fake root matched. Everything it signed was trusted.
The patch: validate the full set of parameters, so a key counts as trusted only on its original curve. Lesson: verify every input to a signature check, not just the key.

blocks.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

signing_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()    # keep this secret
verify_key = signing_key.public_key()         # ship this with the device

firmware = b"firmware v2.0 bytes"
sig = signing_key.sign(firmware)              # 64 bytes
print(len(sig))

# Ed25519 derives its per-signature secret from the key and message,
# so the same message always gives the same signature:
print(sig == signing_key.sign(firmware))     # True

verify_key.verify(sig, firmware)              # passes silently
try:
    verify_key.verify(sig, firmware + b"!")   # one byte added
except InvalidSignature:
    print("rejected")
blocks.caption: Runnable. Ed25519 through the cryptography library: no nonce for you to get wrong, and verify raises on any change.

blocks.md: Defender view. Prevent: prefer Ed25519 or deterministic ECDSA; reject certificates with explicit curve parameters; patch crypto libraries quickly (CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, ordered US agencies to patch CVE-2020-0601 under an emergency directive). Detect: monitor for duplicate r values across signatures, which reveal k reuse. Respond: if k was reused, the private key is gone: revoke, rotate and re-sign.

blocks.question: Two ECDSA signatures from the same key have the same r value. What does that tell you?
options: The same per-message secret k was used, and the private key can be computed from the two signatures
blocks.explain: r is the x-coordinate of kG, so equal r means equal k (for practical purposes). Then the two s equations solve for k and the private key, as with the PS3.

blocks.question: What was the root cause of CurveBall?
options: Certificate validation matched the public key without checking the curve parameters it belonged to
A weak random number generator in Windows
blocks.explain: A public key only means something together with its curve and generator. Accepting attacker-chosen parameters let the attacker choose a generator for which they knew the private key.

lessons.title: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto

blocks.md: No primitive is useful alone. A **protocol** combines them so each covers another's gap. TLS 1.3 (Transport Layer Security, RFC 9846, the protocol behind HTTPS) is the best example to read with everything you now know. Simplified handshake:

blocks.title: TLS 1.3 handshake, mapped to primitives (simplified)

scenes.caption: ClientHello: a fresh random value and an ephemeral (single-use) key share. Today that is usually the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 (RFC 10024): X25519 plus ML-KEM, a post-quantum key exchange. CSPRNG plus key agreement.
ServerHello with its own key share. Both sides now compute the DH shared secret and feed it through the HKDF key schedule.
From here everything is encrypted with an AEAD (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). The server sends its certificate chain, signed by a CA.
CertificateVerify: the server signs the whole handshake transcript with its certificate key. This defeats the DH man in the middle from lesson 13.
Finished messages: an HMAC over the transcript, proving both sides saw the same handshake and nobody altered it.
Application data flows under AEAD with per-direction keys from HKDF. Most primitives in this course appear here: CSPRNG, Diffie-Hellman, HKDF, AEAD, signatures and HMAC.

blocks.code:
import socket, ssl

# RIGHT: the default context checks the certificate chain and the hostname
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
with socket.create_connection(("www.python.org", 443)) as raw:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname="www.python.org") as tls:
        print(tls.version())      # e.g. TLSv1.3
        print(tls.cipher()[0])    # e.g. TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256

# WRONG: turning checks off makes the encryption talk to anyone,
# including an attacker in the middle.
# ctx.check_hostname = False
# ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
blocks.caption: Runnable (needs network). The library does all of the above; your job is to not turn the checks off.

blocks.md:
**The rules**, each tied to a failure you have now seen:

1. **Do not roll your own** algorithm or protocol. Flickr's hash(secret + data) and textbook RSA both look reasonable and both fail.
2. **Use vetted, high-level libraries**: the cryptography library's Fernet or AEAD classes, libsodium (a widely used C library of easy-to-use primitives), Google's Tink, your platform's TLS. Prefer APIs with no nonce or mode for you to choose.
3. **Never reuse a nonce, IV or one-time key** (two-time pad, Böck's 184 servers, the PS3).
4. **Get randomness from the OS CSPRNG** (Debian, time-seeded tokens).
5. **Authenticate before you trust**: AEAD, not bare CBC or CTR; HMAC, not hash(key + data); verify signatures and every parameter (CurveBall).
6. **Compare secrets in constant time** (hmac.compare_digest).
7. **Retire broken algorithms**: MD5, SHA-1, ECB, 3DES, small DH groups (Flame, SHAttered, Adobe).
8. **Hash passwords with a slow salted function**, never encrypt them (Adobe again).
9. **Plan for change**: keep algorithm choices in configuration so you can rotate keys and swap algorithms.

Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

**Practice legally.** Crypto bugs are ideal to learn hands-on because you attack your own toy systems:

- [Cryptopals crypto challenges](https://www.cryptopals.com/): build and break ECB, CBC, CTR, MACs and RSA yourself, in any language.
- [CryptoHack](https://cryptohack.org/): free, browser-based crypto puzzles from XOR to elliptic curves.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/): Carnegie Mellon's free capture-the-flag practice platform (picoCTF renamed in 2026), with beginner challenges and learning paths.

Only test systems you own or have written permission to test.

blocks.question: In TLS 1.3, which message stops a man in the middle from substituting their own Diffie-Hellman key share?
options: The AEAD tag on application data
CertificateVerify, the server's signature over the handshake
blocks.explain: The key shares are just DH values. CertificateVerify signs the transcript, including them, with the key the CA vouched for, so substituted shares fail verification.

blocks.question: A teammate proposes encrypting session cookies with AES-CTR and a counter stored in memory that resets to 0 on restart. Which rule does this break?
options: Never reuse a nonce: after a restart the same counter values repeat under the same key, and CTR also lacks authentication
blocks.explain: A counter that resets repeats keystreams (two-time pad), and plain CTR gives no integrity, so cookies could be bit-flipped. Use an AEAD with random or persistent nonces, or a vetted token library.
